# There Is a Way Around It

The third pre-release for [#57](https://github.com/timmaurice/bergfex/issues/57), and the first one that can tell you what to do about it. `beta.1` made a refused request legible; the evidence it collected then identified the cause, and the cause turns out to have a remedy you can apply yourself.

## What was found

On a live installation with seventeen resorts, five failed and twelve did not. The five had exactly one thing in common: **every one of them ended up on `www.bergfex.de`**, which answered 403 with a Cloudflare block page. Everything on `www.bergfex.at`, `www.bergfex.com`, `www.bergfex.fr` and the rest was served normally, from the same machine, in the same second.

It is not a rate limit — a single entry reloaded on its own was refused eighteen times in a row. It is not your connection, since the other domains answer it fine. It is that one host.

And German resorts reach that host from exactly one place: **the German domain**, which redirects them there. Every other language domain serves the same resort itself and never touches `www.bergfex.de`. That was checked against both a snow report and a cross-country trail report.

## So the repair notice now names the way out

Open one of the affected entries, choose **Reconfigure**, and pick another language — English keeps the readings legible. The entry moves to that language's bergfex domain, the resort is served, and the entities and their history are kept. The readings then arrive in that language, which is the whole of the price.

Verified before it was written down: a resort stuck on 403 was switched to English and came up on the first try. The notice dropped it from its list by itself and stayed up for the ones still refused.

## Also fixed

- **A refusal no longer reads as "check your internet connection".** Adding a resort, or changing an entry's language, asks bergfex whether the page serves first, and every failure collapsed into that one message — which is the wrong advice for somebody whose connection is fine. A refusal now says so, and the Cloudflare ray id goes to the log. The country overview behind "no areas found" reports its refusal too.
- **The daily site check asks the question users ask.** It was sending two real Chrome user agents while the integration is stuck with Home Assistant's own, so it could pass on markup no installation ever receives. It now sends what the integration sends, records refusals instead of hiding them in a retry loop, and reports which host each resort ends up on. A German resort is checked for the first time — which is how this whole class of failure stayed invisible.

## Upgrading

Nothing to do. If some of your resorts are stuck on 403, read the repair notice and try the language switch.
